arXiv:2402.00380v1 [math.NA] 01 Feb 2024

nn-Dimensional Volumetric Stretch Energy Minimization for Volume-/Mass-Preserving Parameterizations

Zhong-Heng Tan    Tiexiang Li    Wen-Wei Lin    Shing-Tung Yau
Abstract

In this paper, we develop an nn dimensional volumetric stretch energy (nn-VSE) functional for the volume-/mass-preserving parameterization of the nn-manifolds topologically equivalent to nn-ball. The nn-VSE has a lower bound and equal to it if and only if the map is volume-/mass-preserving. This motivates us to minimize the nn-VSE to achieve the ideal volume-/mass-preserving parameterization. In the discrete case, we also guarantee the relation between the lower bound and the volume-/mass-preservation, and propose the spherical and ball volume-/mass-preserving parameterization algorithms. The numerical experiments indicate the accuracy and robustness of the proposed algorithms. The modified algorithms are applied to the manifold registration and deformation, showing the versatility of nn-VSE.

Key words— nn dimensional volumetric stretch energy, volume-/mass-preserving map, nn-manifold, spherical parameterization, ball parameterization

MSC(2020) 49Q10, 52C26, 65D18, 65F05, 68U05

1 Introduction

In this paper, we consider ℳ\mathcal{M} as an nn-dimensional manifold which is topologically equivalent to an nn-ball 𝔹n={𝐱∈ℝn|‖𝐱‖22≤1}\mathbb{B}^{n}=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}~|~\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}\leq 1\}. An nn-dimensional parameterization between ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝔹n\mathbb{B}^{n} can be referred as to find a bijective map from ℳ\mathcal{M} to 𝔹n\mathbb{B}^{n}. The mapping induces a canonical coordinate system on the nn-manifold, which can be used to simplify the process issue arising from digital geometrical patterns, and medical image data. In particular, surface (22-manifold) and volume (3-manifold) parameterizations have been widely applied in computer graphics [5], image remeshing [19, 2], morphing [22], registration [12, 17, 24] and texture mapping [1, 15], etc. In recent years, several numerical algorithms from different approaches for the computation of surface [6, 3, 8, 16, 23], or volume [18, 20, 7, 21, 14, 10] parameterizations have been well-developed and proposed by various research groups. Most of parameterization algorithms using nongrid mapping method for surfaces and 3-manifolds are in view of the minimization of distortions of angle or area for 2-manifolds and of volume/mass for 3-manifolds. The corresponding parameterizations, called angle-preserving (conformal), area-preserving (authalic/equiareal) parameterizations, and volume-/mass-preserving parameterizations, are computed by minimizing the Dirichlet energy [22, 11], stretch energy [23] and volumetric stretch energy [20, 21, 9], respectively.

On the other hand, another more general and useful approach, namely, a unifying framework of nn-dimensional quasi-conformal maps [25] to minimize quasi-conformal distortion, volume distortion, landmark mismatch and to ensure the bijectivity and volume prior information for the computation of nn-dimensional quasi-conformal mappings between ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝔹n\mathbb{B}^{n}. More precisely, based on the idea [13], the framework [25] minimizes a generalized conformality distortion to measure the dilation of an nn-dimensional quasi-conformal maps and satisfies the landmark constraints. Furthermore, the orientation constraint (determinant >0>0) is converted into an equality constraint by using the exponential function with adding a regularizer to minimize the volume change. The associated nn-dimensional quasi-conformal maps can be solved by ADMM with O⁡(1k)O(\frac{1}{k}) convergence. The framework [25] can be successfully applied to the adaptive remeshing, graphics and medical image registration.

Based on the techniques of volumetric stretch energy minimization developed in [20, 9], in this paper, we first introduce the nn-dimensional volumetric stretch energy functional on ℳ\mathcal{M} and the associated volumetric stretch Laplacian matrix with modified cotangent weights. We propose the nn-dimensional volumetric stretch energy minimization (nn-VSEM) for the computation of an approximately nn-ball volume-/mass-preserving parameterization from ℳ\mathcal{M} to 𝔹n\mathbb{B}^{n}. The minimal volumetric stretch energy is shown to have the lower bound ν​(𝔹n)2μ⁡(ℳ)\frac{\nu(\mathbb{B}^{n})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})}, where μ\mu and ν\nu are the measure defined on ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝔹n\mathbb{B}^{n}, respectively, and the minimizer forms a volume-/mass-preserving map if and only if the volumetric stretch energy attains this lower bound. This conclusion has been proved in [9] when n=3n=3 as a special case with ν(⋅)=|⋅|\nu(\cdot)=|\cdot|. However, the proof used a too strong constraint |f⁡(ℳ)|=μ⁡(ℳ)|f(\mathcal{M})|=\mu(\mathcal{M}). In this paper, we loose the constraint and give the theorems in continuous and discrete cases. This relationship critically and successfully provides the setting for the modified volumetric stretch energy functional. In fact, nn-VSEM with constraints have some differences with the unifying framework for nn-dimensional quasi-conformal mapping by (i) replacing two distortion and smooth balancing items by a volumetric stretch energy functional with modified cotangent weights; (ii) replacing the ADMM method by the fixed-point type iteration, for which according to numerical experiments, both methods have sublinear convergence rate of O⁡(1k)O(\frac{1}{k});

The main contribution of this paper is four folds.

  • •

    We propose a continuous nn-dimensional volumetric stretch energy (nn-VSE) functional on ℳ\mathcal{M} having the lower bound ν​(𝔹n)2μ⁡(ℳ)\frac{\nu(\mathbb{B}^{n})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})} and show that the minimizer is volume-/mass-preserving if and only if the minimal energy attains ν​(𝔹n)2μ⁡(ℳ)\frac{\nu(\mathbb{B}^{n})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})}.

  • •

    The discrete nn-VSE can be written as a quadratic form with respect to a Laplacian matrix with modified cotangent weights having local sparse connectivity. The stretch energy defined in [23, 20, 21, 9] are equivalent to nn-VSE when n=2n=2 and n=3n=3. A theorem about the lower bound of discrete nn-VSE is proposed as the motivation for the proposed nn-VSEM algorithm.

  • •

    We propose the nn-VSEM algorithm for the efficient computation of ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving parameterization. The constrained optimization problem induced from the lower bound theorem is divided into a small-scale constrained boundary subproblem and a large-scale unconstrained interior subproblem. The boundary subproblem is solved by the Newton method and the interior subproblem is solved by the fixed-point method.

  • •

    In the numerical experiments, we shows a volume-preserving parameterization of the 33 and 44 dimensional ellipsoids as a special case, which indicates the nn-VSE can reach the guaranteed lower bound, that is, the resulting map is mass-preserving. For the general manifold, the proposed algorithm compute the ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving maps with low mass distortion, demonstrating the robustness and accuracy. The application of nn-VSEM on manifold registration and deformation also has a robust performance by the modified algorithms.

2 nn-dimensional Volumetric Stretch Energy

Let ℳ={𝐱=h(𝐮),𝐮=(u1,u2,⋯,un)∈Ω⊆ℝn}\mathcal{M}=\{\mathbf{x}=h(\mathbf{u}),\mathbf{u}=(u_{1},u_{2},\cdots,u_{n})\in\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\} be a smooth nn-manifold topologically equivalent to an nn-dimensional unit ball 𝔹n\mathbb{B}^{n}. Hence the mass of arbitrary subregion B⊂ℳB\subset\mathcal{M} is μ⁡(B)=∫B𝑑μ=∫Bρμ​𝑑σ\mu(B)=\int_{B}d\mu=\int_{B}\rho_{\mu}d\sigma. Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be another nn-manifold topologically equivalent to ℳ\mathcal{M} with ν\nu and ρν\rho_{\nu} being the measure and density function defined in it. The density functions satisfy 0<L≤ρμ,ρν<+∞0<L\leq\rho_{\mu},\rho_{\nu}<+\infty. An orientation preserving and bijective C1C^{1} map f:ℳ→𝒩f:\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{N} is said to be mass-preserving if ν⁡(A)/ν⁡(f⁡(ℳ))=μ⁡(f−1​(A))/μ⁡(ℳ)\nu(A)/\nu(f(\mathcal{M}))=\mu(f^{-1}(A))/\mu(\mathcal{M}) for every subregion A⊂f⁡(ℳ)A\subset f(\mathcal{M}). ν⁡(A)\displaystyle\nu(A) =∫A𝑑ν=∫(f∘h)−1​(A)(ρν∘f∘h)​det(Jf∘h⊤​Jf∘h)​𝑑s,\displaystyle=\int_{A}d\nu=\int_{(f\circ h)^{-1}(A)}(\rho_{\nu}\circ f\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{f\circ h}^{\top}J_{f\circ h})}ds, (2.1)
μ​(f−1​(A))\displaystyle\mu(f^{-1}(A)) =∫f−1​(A)𝑑μ=∫(f∘h)−1​(A)(ρμ∘h)​det(Jh⊤​Jh)​𝑑s,\displaystyle=\int_{f^{-1}(A)}d\mu=\int_{(f\circ h)^{-1}(A)}(\rho_{\mu}\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{h}^{\top}J_{h})}ds, (2.2)

(ρν∘f∘h)​det(Jf∘h⊤​Jf∘h)∫Ω(ρν∘f∘h)​det(Jf∘h⊤​Jf∘h)​𝑑s=(ρμ∘h)​det(Jh⊤​Jh)∫Ω(ρμ∘h)​det(Jh⊤​Jh)​𝑑s,\displaystyle\frac{(\rho_{\nu}\circ f\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{f\circ h}^{\top}J_{f\circ h})}}{\int_{\Omega}(\rho_{\nu}\circ f\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{f\circ h}^{\top}J_{f\circ h})}ds}=\frac{(\rho_{\mu}\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{h}^{\top}J_{h})}}{\int_{\Omega}(\rho_{\mu}\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{h}^{\top}J_{h})}ds}, (2.3)

To find the ideal mass-preserving map ff, we first define the nn-dimensional volumetric stretch energy (nn-VSE) functional of the map ff as

EV​(f)=∫ℳ[ρν∘fρμ​Det​(∇ℳf)]2​𝑑μ,\displaystyle E_{V}(f)=\int_{\mathcal{M}}\left[\frac{\rho_{\nu}\circ f}{\rho_{\mu}}{\rm Det}(\nabla_{\mathcal{M}}f)\right]^{2}d\mu, (2.4)

Remark 1.

In (2.7), the formula det(Jh⊤​Jh)\sqrt{\det(J_{h}^{\top}J_{h})} represents the volume ratio of h⁡(τ)h(\tau) to τ\tau with τ\tau being a infinitesimal region on Ω\Omega, that is, det(Jh⊤​Jh)=lim|τ|→0|h⁡(τ)||τ|\sqrt{\det(J_{h}^{\top}J_{h})}=\lim_{|\tau|\to 0}\frac{|h(\tau)|}{|\tau|}. Similarly, we also have det(Jf∘h⊤​Jf∘h)=lim|τ|→0|f∘h⁡(τ)||τ|\sqrt{\det(J_{f\circ h}^{\top}J_{f\circ h})}=\lim_{|\tau|\to 0}\frac{|f\circ h(\tau)|}{|\tau|}. Hence, from the derivation in (2.6), Det⁡(∇ℳf){\rm Det}(\nabla_{\mathcal{M}}f) means the volume ratio of the f∘h⁡(τ)f\circ h(\tau) on 𝒩\mathcal{N} to h⁡(τ)h(\tau) on ℳ\mathcal{M}. In the geometric perspective, letting σ=h⁡(τ)\sigma=h(\tau), the nn-VSE is the sum of square of the mass ratios of each image infinitesimal region f⁡(σ)f(\sigma) to the origin infinitesimal region σ\sigma in ℳ\mathcal{M}. In other words,

EV​(f)=limμ⁡(σ)→0∑σ⊂ℳ[ν⁡(f⁡(σ))μ⁡(σ)]2​μ​(σ)\displaystyle E_{V}(f)=\lim_{\mu(\sigma)\to 0}\sum_{\sigma\subset\mathcal{M}}\left[\frac{\nu(f(\sigma))}{\mu(\sigma)}\right]^{2}\mu(\sigma) (2.9)

.

Using the representation (2.8), we give a significant theorem for the lower bound of the nn-VSE.

Theorem 1.

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be an nn-manifold to be topologically equivalent to 𝒩\mathcal{N}, μ\mu and ν\nu be the measures defined on ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝒩\mathcal{N}, ρμ\rho_{\mu} and ρν\rho_{\nu} be the corresponding densities. For nn-VSE EV​(f)E_{V}(f) defined in (2.4), let

Sf={EV(f)|f:ℳ→𝒩 is an orientation preserving and bijective C1 map with f(∂ℳ)=∂𝒩}.\displaystyle S_{f}=\left\{E_{V}(f)~|~f:\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{N}\text{ is an orientation preserving and bijective $C^{1}$ map with }f(\partial\mathcal{M})=\partial\mathcal{N}\right\}. (2.10)

Then we have

  • (i)

    min⁡Sf≥ν​(𝒩)2μ⁡(ℳ)\min S_{f}\geq\frac{\nu(\mathcal{N})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})};

  • (ii)

    f∗=argminSf=ν​(𝒩)2μ⁡(ℳ)f^{*}=\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}S_{f}=\frac{\nu(\mathcal{N})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})} if and only if f∗f^{*} is mass-preserving.

Proof.

For the representation of the nn-VSE in (2.8), we treat (ρν∘f∘h)​det(Jf∘h⊤​Jf∘h)(\rho_{\nu}\circ f\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{f\circ h}^{\top}J_{f\circ h})} as the variable ξ\xi. The nn-VSE becomes

EV​(ξ)=∫Ωξ2(ρμ∘h)​det(Jh⊤​Jh)​𝑑s.\displaystyle E_{V}(\xi)=\int_{\Omega}\frac{\xi^{2}}{(\rho_{\mu}\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{h}^{\top}J_{h})}}ds. (2.11)

Consider the problem

minξSξ:={EV(ξ)|∫Ωξds=ν(𝒩),ξ≥0}.\displaystyle\min_{\xi}S_{\xi}:=\left\{E_{V}(\xi)\left|\int_{\Omega}\xi ds=\nu(\mathcal{N}),\xi\geq 0\right.\right\}. (2.12)

By Euler-Lagrange equation, we have

2​ξ(ρμ∘h)​det(Jh⊤​Jh)+λ=0.\displaystyle\frac{2\xi}{(\rho_{\mu}\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{h}^{\top}J_{h})}}+\lambda=0. (2.13)

It follows that 2​ξ=−λ⁡(ρμ∘h)​det(Jh⊤​Jh)2\xi=-\lambda(\rho_{\mu}\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{h}^{\top}J_{h})}. Integrating the both sides and using the equalities ν⁡(𝒩)=ν⁡(f⁡(ℳ))=∫Ωξ​𝑑s\nu(\mathcal{N})=\nu(f(\mathcal{M}))=\int_{\Omega}\xi ds and μ⁡(ℳ)=∫Ω(ρμ∘h)​det(Jh⊤​Jh)​𝑑s\mu(\mathcal{M})=\int_{\Omega}(\rho_{\mu}\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{h}^{\top}J_{h})}ds, we have λ=−2ν(𝒩)/μ(ℳ)\lambda=-2\nu(\mathcal{N})/\mu(\mathcal{M}). Then substituting this formula into (2.13), it follows that ξ=ν⁡(𝔹n)​(ρμ∘h)​det(Jh⊤​Jh)μ⁡(ℳ)\xi=\frac{\nu(\mathbb{B}^{n})(\rho_{\mu}\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{h}^{\top}J_{h})}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})}. That is

(ρν∘f∘h)​det(Jf∘h⊤​Jf∘h)ν⁡(𝒩)=ξν⁡(𝒩)=(ρμ∘h)​det(Jh⊤​Jh)μ⁡(ℳ),\displaystyle\frac{(\rho_{\nu}\circ f\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{f\circ h}^{\top}J_{f\circ h})}}{\nu(\mathcal{N})}=\frac{\xi}{\nu(\mathcal{N})}=\frac{(\rho_{\mu}\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{h}^{\top}J_{h})}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})}, (2.14)

which means the mass-preservation. Additionally, it is easy to verify that the optimization problem (2.12) is convex. Therefore, the solution of the Euler-Lagrange equation is the minimizer of the optimization problem (2.12) and hence minξ⁡Sξ=ν​(𝒩)2μ⁡(ℳ)\min_{\xi}S_{\xi}=\frac{\nu(\mathcal{N})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})}. Since Sf⊆SξS_{f}\subseteq S_{\xi}, we have

minf⁡Sf≥minξ⁡Sξ=ν​(𝒩)2μ⁡(ℳ),\displaystyle\min_{f}S_{f}\geq\min_{\xi}S_{\xi}=\frac{\nu(\mathcal{N})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})}, (2.15)

completing the proof of (i). Meanwhile, (2.14) implies that minf⁡Sf\min_{f}S_{f} reaches the lower bound ν​(𝒩)2μ⁡(ℳ)\frac{\nu(\mathcal{N})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})} if and only if the resulting map f∗f^{*} is mass-preserving. Hence, (ii) is proved. ∎

For the parameterization problem, (i) in the theorem 1 gives a lower bound of the nn-VSE under the constraint f⁡(ℳ)=𝒩f(\mathcal{M})=\mathcal{N}. Meanwhile, (ii) tells that the nn-VSE reaches this lower bound only when the map is mass-preserving. This motivate us to seek for the ideal mass-preserving parameterization via the nn-VSE minimization problem.

However, it is worth noting that the existence and uniqueness of such a mass-preserving map from ℳ\mathcal{M} to 𝔹n\mathbb{B}^{n} are not theoretically guaranteed. The mass-preserving map absolutely satisfying the conditions in (3.38) for the given manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} does not necessarily exist. Furthermore, even if the mass-preserving map exists, it is not necessarily unique. Taking the unit disk ℳ=𝔹1\mathcal{M}=\mathbb{B}^{1} as instance, we can consider the map ff in the polar coordinates (rf,θf)=(rv,θv+k​rv)(r_{f},\theta_{f})=(r_{v},\theta_{v}+kr_{v}), where k∈ℝk\in\mathbb{R} is a parameter, v=(rvcosθv,rvsinθv)v=(r_{v}\cos\theta_{v},r_{v}\sin\theta_{v}) and f(v)=(rfcosθf,rfsinθf)f(v)=(r_{f}\cos\theta_{f},r_{f}\sin\theta_{f}). We can confirm that f:𝔹1→𝔹1f:\mathbb{B}^{1}\to\mathbb{B}^{1} and

det(Jf)=det(∂f∂(rf,θf))​det(∂(rf,θf)∂(rv,θv))​det(∂v∂(rv,θv))−1=det(∂(rf,θf)∂(rv,θv))=1.\displaystyle\det(J_{f})=\det\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial(r_{f},\theta_{f})}\right)\det\left(\frac{\partial(r_{f},\theta_{f})}{\partial(r_{v},\theta_{v})}\right)\det\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial(r_{v},\theta_{v})}\right)^{-1}=\det\left(\frac{\partial(r_{f},\theta_{f})}{\partial(r_{v},\theta_{v})}\right)=1. (2.16)

Hence, the constructed map ff is an area-preserving map and we can select different parameters kk to obtain different area-preserving maps. As shown in Figure 1, we plots the cases k=0,1,3k=0,1,3. When k=0k=0, ff is identity map. When k=1,3k=1,3, the red lines in Figure 1a become the curves in Figure 1b and Figure 1c, while the areas of the parts formed by the curves remain π/6\pi/6.

Practically, we cannot expect an ideally mass-preserving and unique map as above mentioned. Hence, we take a step back and aim to find a mass-preserving as possible map for the given nn-manifold ℳ\mathcal{M}. To measure the degree of mass-preservation, we define the mass-preserving error of a map ff as

ε=EV​(f)−ν​(𝔹n)2μ⁡(ℳ)\displaystyle\varepsilon=E_{V}(f)-\frac{\nu(\mathbb{B}^{n})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})} (2.17)

and find an approximately mass-preserving map, named ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving map.

Definition 1.

A map f:ℳ→𝔹nf:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{B}^{n} is an ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving map if ε=EV​(f)−ν​(𝔹n)2μ⁡(ℳ)\varepsilon=E_{V}(f)-\frac{\nu(\mathbb{B}^{n})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})}.

Then, we further give the following theorem to show the measurement of the mass-preserving error ε\varepsilon.

Theorem 2.

Let f:ℳ→𝔹nf:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{B}^{n} be an orientation preserving and bijective C1C^{1} map with f⁡(∂ℳ)=𝕊n−1f(\partial\mathcal{M})=\mathbb{S}^{n-1} and ε=EV​(f)−ν​(𝔹n)2μ⁡(ℳ)\varepsilon=E_{V}(f)-\frac{\nu(\mathbb{B}^{n})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})} and

δ=(ρν∘f)/ν⁡(𝔹n)ρμ/μ⁡(ℳ)​Det​(∇ℳf)−1.\displaystyle\delta=\frac{\nicefrac{{(\rho_{\nu}\circ f)}}{{\nu(\mathbb{B}^{n})}}}{\nicefrac{{\rho_{\mu}}}{{\mu(\mathcal{M})}}}{\rm Det}(\nabla_{\mathcal{M}}f)-1. (2.18)

Then

ε=ν​(𝔹n)2μ​(ℳ)2​‖δ‖L2​(ℳ)2.\displaystyle\varepsilon=\frac{\nu(\mathbb{B}^{n})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})^{2}}\|\delta\|_{L^{2}(\mathcal{M})}^{2}. (2.19)
Proof.

Let

ξ~=(ρν∘f∘h)​det(Jf∘h⊤​Jf∘h)ν⁡(𝔹n),μ~=(ρμ∘h)​det(Jh⊤​Jh)μ⁡(ℳ),\displaystyle\tilde{\xi}=\frac{(\rho_{\nu}\circ f\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{f\circ h}^{\top}J_{f\circ h})}}{\nu(\mathbb{B}^{n})},\hskip 9.24994pt\tilde{\mu}=\frac{(\rho_{\mu}\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{h}^{\top}J_{h})}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})}, (2.20)
μ~max:=max⁡μ~=μmaxμ⁡(ℳ),\displaystyle\tilde{\mu}_{\text{max}}:=\max\tilde{\mu}=\frac{\mu_{\text{max}}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})}, (2.21)

Then δ=ξ~/μ~−1\delta=\tilde{\xi}/\tilde{\mu}-1 and

∫Ωξ~​𝑑s=∫Ωμ~​𝑑s=1.\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\tilde{\xi}ds=\int_{\Omega}\tilde{\mu}ds=1. (2.23)

Using this equality and (2.8), we have

ε=\displaystyle\varepsilon= EV​(f)−ν​(𝔹n)2μ⁡(ℳ)=ν​(𝔹n)2μ⁡(ℳ)​[∫Ωμ~​(δ+1)2​𝑑s−1]\displaystyle E_{V}(f)-\frac{\nu(\mathbb{B}^{n})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})}=\frac{\nu(\mathbb{B}^{n})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})}\left[\int_{\Omega}\tilde{\mu}(\delta+1)^{2}ds-1\right] (2.24)
=\displaystyle= ν​(𝔹n)2μ⁡(ℳ)​∫Ωμ~​[(δ+1)2−1]​𝑑s=ν​(𝔹n)2μ⁡(ℳ)​∫Ωμ~​δ2​𝑑s\displaystyle\frac{\nu(\mathbb{B}^{n})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})}\int_{\Omega}\tilde{\mu}[(\delta+1)^{2}-1]ds=\frac{\nu(\mathbb{B}^{n})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})}\int_{\Omega}\tilde{\mu}\delta^{2}ds (2.25)
=\displaystyle= ν​(𝔹n)2μ​(ℳ)2​∫ℳδ2​𝑑μ=ν​(𝔹n)2μ​(ℳ)2​‖δ‖L2​(ℳ)2.\displaystyle\frac{\nu(\mathbb{B}^{n})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})^{2}}\int_{\mathcal{M}}\delta^{2}d\mu=\frac{\nu(\mathbb{B}^{n})^{2}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})^{2}}\|\delta\|_{L^{2}(\mathcal{M})}^{2}. (2.26)

∎

The term δ2\delta^{2} is the square of the relative error of (ρν∘f∘h)​det(Jf∘h⊤​Jf∘h)ν⁡(𝔹n)\frac{(\rho_{\nu}\circ f\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{f\circ h}^{\top}J_{f\circ h})}}{\nu(\mathbb{B}^{n})} and (ρμ∘h)​det(Jh⊤​Jh)μ⁡(ℳ)\frac{(\rho_{\mu}\circ h)\sqrt{\det(J_{h}^{\top}J_{h})}}{\mu(\mathcal{M})}, which can represent a local error at a point in ℳ\mathcal{M}. From (2.26) we can find that ε\varepsilon is equivalent to the sum of all local errors δ2\delta^{2} among the manifold ℳ\mathcal{M}. Hence, it is appropriate to choose ε\varepsilon as the measurement. In this paper, we aim to find the ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving map with as small error ε\varepsilon as possible via minimizing SfS_{f} in (2.10).

Remark 2.

For ∂ℳ\partial\mathcal{M} topologically equivalent to 𝒮n−1\mathcal{S}^{n-1} and the map f:∂ℳ→𝒮n−1f:\partial\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{S}^{n-1}, we can also give the similar theorems to Theorem 1 and Theorem 2. The theorems and proofs are almost identical and hence not worth being repeated.

3 Discrete nn-Manifold and nn-Volumetric Stretch Energy

Now, we focus on the algorithm for the mass-preserving parameterization. At first, we introduce the manifolds in triangular mesh and the nn-VSE in the discrete perspective. The notations used in the previous section will be abused without being misinterpreted to represent the discrete notations. In this paper, we consider the mass-preserving parameterization to the nn-ball with ρν=1\rho_{\nu}=1. Therefore, in the discrete case, we let ν(⋅)=|⋅|\nu(\cdot)=|\cdot| and ρ:=ρμ\rho:=\rho_{\mu} for simplicity.

3.1 Discrete nn-Manifold

The discrete nn-manifold discussed in this paper is composed of simplices. We first give the definitions of the discrete nn-manifold and the related nn-simplex.

Definition 2.

(1) Let {v0,v1,⋯,vk}⊆ℝn\{v_{0},v_{1},\cdots,v_{k}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} with k≤nk\leq n. A kk-simplex σ=[v0,v1,⋯,vk]\sigma=[v_{0},v_{1},\cdots,v_{k}] is defined by

σ=[v0,v1,⋯,vk]={𝐱∈ℝn|𝐱=∑i=0kαivi,∑i=0kαi=1,αi≥0}.\displaystyle\sigma=[v_{0},v_{1},\cdots,v_{k}]=\left\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}~\Bigg|~\mathbf{x}=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\alpha_{i}v_{i},\sum_{i=0}^{k}\alpha_{i}=1,\alpha_{i}\geq 0\right\}. (3.1)

An ℓ\ell-facet fa​(σ)f_{a}(\sigma) of σ\sigma with ℓ<k\ell<k is defined as fa​(σ)={τ⊆σ|τ​ is an ℓ-simplex}f_{a}(\sigma)=\{\tau\subseteq\sigma~|~\tau\text{ is an $\ell$-simplex}\}. v0,⋯,vkv_{0},\cdots,v_{k} are called the vertices of the kk-simplex σ\sigma. Suppose τ⊂σ\tau\subset\sigma is also an ℓ\ell-simplex (ℓ<n\ell<n), then τ\tau is an ℓ\ell-facet of σ\sigma. Let fa​(σ)f_{a}(\sigma) denote the set of all facets of σ\sigma.

(2) A simplicial nn-complex SS is a union of nn-simplices such that (i) if an nn-simplex belongs to SS, all its facets also belongs to SS; (ii) if σ1,σ2∈S\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\in S, σ1∩σ2≠∅\sigma_{1}\cap\sigma_{2}\neq\varnothing (empty set), σ1∩σ2∈fa​(σ1)\sigma_{1}\cap\sigma_{2}\in f_{a}(\sigma_{1}) and fa​(σ2)f_{a}(\sigma_{2}).

(3) The link of a vertex v∈Sv\in S is the union of (n−1)(n-1)-simplex τ∈S\tau\in S with v∉τv\notin\tau and [v,τ][v,\tau] being an nn-simplex of SS.

(4) v∈Sv\in S is an interior vertex, if the link of vv is topologically equivalent to 𝕊n−1\mathbb{S}^{n-1}; otherwise vv is a boundary vertex.

Definition 3.

(1) A discrete nn-manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} is a simplicial nn-complex which is topologically equivalent to 𝔹n\mathbb{B}^{n}.

(2) ∂ℳ\partial\mathcal{M} is a discrete (n−1)(n-1)-manifold which consists of all (n−1)(n-1)-facets of ℳ\mathcal{M} with all vertices being boundary vertices.

The discrete nn-manifold has some properties.

Property 1.

(1) ∂ℳ\partial\mathcal{M} is topologically equivalent to 𝕊n−1\mathbb{S}^{n-1}.

(2) If v∈ℳv\in\mathcal{M} is an interior vertex, the link of vv is topologically equivalent to 𝕊n−1\mathbb{S}^{n-1}. If v∈∂ℳv\in\partial\mathcal{M} is a boundary vertex of ℳ\mathcal{M}, the link of vv on ∂ℳ\partial\mathcal{M} is topologically equivalent to 𝕊n−2\mathbb{S}^{n-2}.

A discrete nn-manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} has NN vertices

𝕊0(ℳ)={vi=(vi1,vi2,⋯,vin)∈ℝn}i=1N\displaystyle\mathbb{S}_{0}(\mathcal{M})=\{v_{i}=(v_{i}^{1},v_{i}^{2},\cdots,v_{i}^{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\}_{i=1}^{N}

and the set of nn-simplex 𝕊n​(ℳ)\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M}) and the set of kk-facets 𝕊k​(ℳ)\mathbb{S}_{k}(\mathcal{M}), for k<nk<n, are defined as follows.

𝕊n(ℳ)={[vi0,vi1,⋯,vin]⊆ℝn for some vij∈𝕊0(ℳ),j=0,1,⋯,n}.\displaystyle\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})=\big\{[v_{i_{0}},v_{i_{1}},\cdots,v_{i_{n}}]\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\text{ for some }v_{i_{j}}\in\mathbb{S}_{0}(\mathcal{M}),~j=0,1,\cdots,n\big\}. (3.2)

For k<nk<n,

𝕊k​(ℳ)={[vi0,vi1,⋯,vik]⊆ℝn|[vi0,vi1,⋯,vik,vik+1]∈𝕊k+1​(ℳ)​ with some ​vik+1∈𝕊0​(ℳ)}.\displaystyle\mathbb{S}_{k}(\mathcal{M})=\big\{[v_{i_{0}},v_{i_{1}},\cdots,v_{i_{k}}]\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}~|~[v_{i_{0}},v_{i_{1}},\cdots,v_{i_{k}},v_{i_{k+1}}]\in\mathbb{S}_{k+1}(\mathcal{M})\text{ with some }v_{i_{k+1}}\in\mathbb{S}_{0}(\mathcal{M})\big\}. (3.3)

For every τ∈𝕊k​(ℳ)\tau\in\mathbb{S}_{k}(\mathcal{M}), there is σ∈𝕊p​(ℳ)\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{p}(\mathcal{M}) such that τ⊂σ\tau\subset\sigma for k<p≤nk<p\leq n.

Since an affine map in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} is determined by n+1n+1 independent point correspondences, a piecewise affine map f:ℳ→ℝnf:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} on an nn-simplex mesh ℳ\mathcal{M} can be expressed as an N×nN\times n matrix defined by the images f⁡(vi)f(v_{i}), where vi∈𝕊0​(ℳ)v_{i}\in\mathbb{S}_{0}(\mathcal{M}), as

𝐟=[𝐟1⊤,𝐟2⊤,⋯,𝐟N⊤]⊤=[𝐟1,𝐟2,⋯,𝐟n]∈ℝN×n,\displaystyle\mathbf{f}=[\mathbf{f}_{1}^{\top},\mathbf{f}_{2}^{\top},\cdots,\mathbf{f}_{N}^{\top}]^{\top}=[\mathbf{f}^{1},\mathbf{f}^{2},\cdots,\mathbf{f}^{n}]\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n}, (3.4)

where 𝐟s=[f1s,f2s,⋯,fNs]⊤∈ℝN×1\mathbf{f}^{s}=[f_{1}^{s},f_{2}^{s},\cdots,f_{N}^{s}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 1}, s=1,2,⋯,ns=1,2,\cdots,n, and 𝐟t=f⁡(vt)=(ft1,ft2,⋯,ftn)∈ℝ1×n\mathbf{f}_{t}=f(v_{t})=(f^{1}_{t},f^{2}_{t},\cdots,f^{n}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times n}, for t=1,2,⋯,Nt=1,2,\cdots,N. For each point v∈𝕊0​(ℳ)v\in\mathbb{S}_{0}(\mathcal{M}), vv must lie into an nn-simplex σ=[v0,v1,⋯,vn]\sigma=[v_{0},v_{1},\cdots,v_{n}] without loss of generality. The piecewise affine map f:ℳ→ℝnf:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} can be expressed as a linear combination of {𝐟i}i=0n\{\mathbf{f}_{i}\}_{i=0}^{n} with the barycentric coordinates

f|σ​(v)=∑i=0nαi​f​(vi),αi=1|σ|​|[v0,⋯,v^i,⋯,vn]|,\displaystyle f\big|_{\sigma}(v)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\alpha_{i}f(v_{i}),\hskip 9.24994pt\alpha_{i}=\frac{1}{|\sigma|}\big|[v_{0},\cdots,\hat{v}_{i},\cdots,v_{n}]\big|, (3.5)

where v^i\hat{v}_{i} is replaced by vv, for i=0,1,⋯,ni=0,1,\cdots,n and |σ||\sigma| denotes the volume of the nn-simplex σ\sigma. To prevent folding of nn-simplex and guarantee the bijectivity via transformation, in this paper, we require the map ff to be solved that preserves the orientation, i.e. f⁡(ℳ)f(\mathcal{M}) is a simplicial nn-complex. In the following discussion, the nn-manifold is that topologically equivalent to an nn-ball, and the (n−1)(n-1)-manifold is that topologically equivalent to an (n−1)(n-1)-sphere.

3.2 Discrete Volumetric Stretch Energy

For the discrete nn-manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} embedded in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and the piecewise affine map f:ℳ→𝔹n⊂ℝnf:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{B}^{n}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, it is easy to verify that the Jacobian matrix Jf−1J_{f^{-1}} satisfies

det(Jf−1|f⁡(σ)):=∫f⁡(σ)det(Jf−1)​𝑑s=|σ||f⁡(σ)|\displaystyle\det\left(J_{f^{-1}}\big|_{f(\sigma)}\right):=\int_{f(\sigma)}\det\left(J_{f^{-1}}\right)ds=\frac{|\sigma|}{|f(\sigma)|} (3.6)

for all σ=[v0,v1,⋯,vn]∈𝕊n​(ℳ)\sigma=[v_{0},v_{1},\cdots,v_{n}]\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M}). This is the ratio of volumes of the nn-simplex and its image simplex. Hence, like the continuous case, the piecewise affine map f:ℳ→ℝnf:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} is said to be induced by 𝐟\mathbf{f} and is volume-preserving if the Jacobian Jf−1J_{f^{-1}} satisfies det(Jf−1|f⁡(σ))=|ℳ||f⁡(ℳ)|\det\left(J_{f^{-1}}\big|_{f(\sigma)}\right)=\frac{|\mathcal{M}|}{|f(\mathcal{M})|}, that is |σ|/|ℳ|=|f⁡(σ)|/|f⁡(ℳ)|\nicefrac{{|\sigma|}}{{|\mathcal{M}|}}=\nicefrac{{|f(\sigma)|}}{{|f(\mathcal{M})|}}. Additionally, let the density function ρ\rho defined in ℳ\mathcal{M} be piecewise constant and the mass μ⁡(σ)=ρ⁡(σ)​|σ|\mu(\sigma)=\rho(\sigma)|\sigma|. The map f:ℳ→ℝnf:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} is mass-preserving if and only if ρ⁡(σ)​det(Jf−1|f⁡(σ))=μ⁡(ℳ)|f⁡(ℳ)|\rho(\sigma)\det\left(J_{f^{-1}}\big|_{f(\sigma)}\right)=\frac{\mu(\mathcal{M})}{|f(\mathcal{M})|}, that is, μ⁡(σ)/μ⁡(ℳ)=|f⁡(σ)|/|f⁡(ℳ)|\nicefrac{{\mu(\sigma)}}{{\mu(\mathcal{M})}}=\nicefrac{{|f(\sigma)|}}{{|f(\mathcal{M})|}}. The Jacobian determinant is an important quantity to measure the mass-preservation. As far as ρ⁡(σ)​det(Jf−1|f⁡(σ))=μ⁡(σ)|f⁡(σ)|\rho(\sigma)\det\left(J_{f^{-1}}\big|_{f(\sigma)}\right)=\frac{\mu(\sigma)}{|f(\sigma)|} is constant for all σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M}), the map ff is mass-preserving. In [23, 20, 9], it is termed the stretch factor as

σμ,f−1​(σ)=ρ⁡(σ)​det(Jf−1|f⁡(σ))=μ⁡(σ)|f⁡(σ)|,\displaystyle\sigma_{\mu,f^{-1}}(\sigma)=\rho(\sigma)\det\left(J_{f^{-1}}\big|_{f(\sigma)}\right)=\frac{\mu(\sigma)}{|f(\sigma)|}, (3.7)

and expected to be a constant. Using the stretch factor, [23, 20, 9] have defined the 22-dimensional stretch energy and 33-dimensional stretch energy and given some theorems and properties associated to the stretch energy when n=2n=2 and 33. Now, we generalize the stretch energy into nn-dimensional and define the discrete nn-dimensional volumetric stretch energy functional as

EV​(f)=1n​trace​(𝐟⊤​LV​(f)​𝐟)=1n​∑s=1n𝐟s⊤​LV​(f)​𝐟s,\displaystyle E_{V}(f)=\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{trace}\big(\mathbf{f}^{\top}L_{V}(f)\mathbf{f}\big)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{s=1}^{n}{\mathbf{f}^{s}}^{\top}L_{V}(f)\mathbf{f}^{s}, (3.8)

where LV​(f)L_{V}(f) is a volumetric stretch symmetric Laplacian matrix with

[LV​(f)]i​j={−wi​j​(f),if ​[vi,vj]∈𝕊1​(ℳ),∑ℓ≠iwi​ℓ​(f),if ​i=j,0,otherwise.\big[L_{V}(f)\big]_{ij}=\begin{cases}-w_{ij}(f),&\text{if }[v_{i},v_{j}]\in\mathbb{S}_{1}(\mathcal{M}),\\ \sum_{\ell\neq i}w_{i\ell}(f),&\text{if }i=j,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (3.9a)

in which the modified cotangent weights wi​j​(f)w_{ij}(f) is defined by

wi​j(f)=1n⁡(n−1)∑[vi,vj]∈𝕊1​(σ)|f⁡(σi^​j^)|σμ,f−1​(σ)cotθi​jσ(f)w_{ij}(f)=\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{[v_{i},v_{j}]\in\mathbb{S}_{1}(\sigma)}\frac{|f(\sigma_{\hat{i}\hat{j}})|}{\sigma_{\mu,f^{-1}}(\sigma)}\cot\theta_{ij}^{\sigma}(f) (3.10a)

with σi^​j^\sigma_{\hat{i}\hat{j}} being the (n−2)(n-2)-simplex containing the vertices 𝕊0​(σ)∖{vi,vj}\mathbb{S}_{0}(\sigma)\setminus\{v_{i},v_{j}\} and θi​jσ​(f)\theta_{ij}^{\sigma}(f) being the dihedral angle between subspaces UiU_{i} and UjU_{j} containing 𝕊0​(f⁡(σ))∖{𝐟i}\mathbb{S}_{0}(f(\sigma))\setminus\{\mathbf{f}_{i}\} and 𝕊0​(f⁡(σ))∖{𝐟j}\mathbb{S}_{0}(f(\sigma))\setminus\{\mathbf{f}_{j}\} respectively.

In the Theorem 3, we will illustrate that this definition in (3.8) is equivalent to our defined nn-VSE in (2.4) in the discrete form

EV​(f)=∫ℳDet​(∇ℳf)2ρ​𝑑s=∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)|f⁡(σ)|2μ⁡(σ).\displaystyle E_{V}(f)=\int_{\mathcal{M}}\frac{{\rm Det}(\nabla_{\mathcal{M}}f)^{2}}{\rho}ds=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\frac{|f(\sigma)|^{2}}{\mu(\sigma)}. (3.11)

To proof this theorem, we first generalize the Dirichlet energy to nn-dimension and give some lemmas associated with it. For the smooth nn-manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} and the orientation preserving and bijective C1C^{1} map f:ℳ→ℝnf:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}, the nn-dimensional Dirichlet energy functional with respect to ff is defined as

ED​(f)=1n​∫ℳ‖∇ℳf‖F2​𝑑s,\displaystyle E_{D}(f)=\frac{1}{n}\int_{\mathcal{M}}\|\nabla_{\mathcal{M}}f\|_{F}^{2}ds, (3.12)

In the discrete case, we consider the discrete nn-manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} and the piecewise affine map ff. The discrete Dirichlet energy is formulated as a quadratic form.

Lemma 1.

Suppose ℳ\mathcal{M} is a discrete nn-manifold embedded in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and ff defined on ℳ\mathcal{M} is a piecewise affine map. Then the nn-dimensional Dirichlet energy defined in (3.12) can be formulated as

ED​(f)=1n​trace​(𝐟⊤​LD​𝐟),\displaystyle E_{D}(f)=\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{f}^{\top}L_{D}\mathbf{f}), (3.13)

where

[LD]i​j={−w~i​j,if ​[vi,vj]∈𝕊1​(ℳ),∑ℓ≠iw~i​j,if ​i=j,0,otherwise.\displaystyle\big[L_{D}\big]_{ij}=\begin{cases}-\tilde{w}_{ij},&\textrm{if }[v_{i},v_{j}]\in\mathbb{S}_{1}(\mathcal{M}),\\ \sum_{\ell\neq i}\tilde{w}_{ij},&\textrm{if }i=j,\\ 0,&\textrm{otherwise.}\end{cases} (3.14)

with the cotangent weight

w~i​j=1n⁡(n−1)∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ):{vi,vj}⊂σ|σi^​j^|cotθi​jσ,\displaystyle\tilde{w}_{ij}=\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M}):\{v_{i},v_{j}\}\subset\sigma}|\sigma_{\hat{i}\hat{j}}|\cot\theta_{ij}^{\sigma}, (3.15)

in which θi​jσ\theta_{ij}^{\sigma} is the dihedral angle between subspaces containing 𝕊0​(σ)∖{vi}\mathbb{S}_{0}(\sigma)\setminus\{v_{i}\} and 𝕊0​(σ)∖{vj}\mathbb{S}_{0}(\sigma)\setminus\{v_{j}\} respectively.

Proof.

Let qq be a point in the nn-simplex σ=[v0,v1,⋯,vn]∈𝕊n​(ℳ)\sigma=[v_{0},v_{1},\cdots,v_{n}]\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M}). f⁡(q)f(q) can be represented by the barycentre coordinates according to (3.5)

f⁡(q)=∑i=0nαi​(q)​𝐟i,αi​(q)=1|σ|​|[v0,⋯,vi−1,q,vi+1,⋯,vn]|.\displaystyle f(q)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\alpha_{i}(q)\mathbf{f}_{i},\hskip 9.24994pt\alpha_{i}(q)=\frac{1}{|\sigma|}\big|[v_{0},\cdots,v_{i-1},q,v_{i+1},\cdots,v_{n}]\big|. (3.16)

For the discrete nn-manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} embedded in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and the piecewise affine map ff, we have ∇ℳf=∇f\nabla_{\mathcal{M}}f=\nabla f. In addition, ∇f\nabla f is a piecewise constant function and can be also represented by the barycentre coordinates as

∇f=∑i=0n𝐟i⊤∇αi.\displaystyle\nabla f=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\mathbf{f}_{i}^{\top}\nabla\alpha_{i}. (3.17)

The volume of the simplex in (3.16) can be expressed as

|[v0,⋯,vi−1,q,vi+1,⋯,vn]|=1n​|σi^|​hiσ​(q),\displaystyle\big|[v_{0},\cdots,v_{i-1},q,v_{i+1},\cdots,v_{n}]\big|=\frac{1}{n}\big|\sigma_{\hat{i}}\big|h_{i}^{\sigma}(q), (3.18)

where hiσ​(q)=(q−vℓ)⊤​n→ih_{i}^{\sigma}(q)=(q-v_{\ell})^{\top}\vec{n}_{i}, ℓ≠i\ell\neq i, is the height corresponding to the face σi^\sigma_{\hat{i}}, whose gradient with respect to qq is n→i∈ℝ1×n\vec{n}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times n}, the inward unit normal vector of the face σi^\sigma_{\hat{i}}. ∇αi=∇|[v0,⋯,vi−1,q,vi+1,⋯,vn]||σ|=1n​|σ|​|σi^|​n→i.\displaystyle\nabla\alpha_{i}=\frac{\nabla\big|[v_{0},\cdots,v_{i-1},q,v_{i+1},\cdots,v_{n}]\big|}{|\sigma|}=\frac{1}{n|\sigma|}|\sigma_{\hat{i}}|\vec{n}_{i}. (3.19)

Hence,

‖∇f‖F2\displaystyle\|\nabla f\|^{2}_{F} =‖∑i=0n𝐟i∇αi‖F2=‖∑i=0n|σi^|n​|σ|𝐟i⊤n→i‖F2\displaystyle=\left\|\sum_{i=0}^{n}\mathbf{f}_{i}\nabla\alpha_{i}\right\|^{2}_{F}=\left\|\sum_{i=0}^{n}\frac{|\sigma_{\hat{i}}|}{n|\sigma|}\mathbf{f}_{i}^{\top}\vec{n}_{i}\right\|^{2}_{F} (3.20)
=∑i=0n∑j=0n|σi^|​|σj^|n2​|σ|2​⟨𝐟i⊤​n→i,𝐟j⊤​n→j⟩=∑i=0n∑j=0n|σi^|​|σj^|n2​|σ|2​(n→i​n→j⊤)​(𝐟i​𝐟j⊤)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\sum_{j=0}^{n}\frac{|\sigma_{\hat{i}}||\sigma_{\hat{j}}|}{n^{2}|\sigma|^{2}}\langle\mathbf{f}_{i}^{\top}\vec{n}_{i},\mathbf{f}_{j}^{\top}\vec{n}_{j}\rangle=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\sum_{j=0}^{n}\frac{|\sigma_{\hat{i}}||\sigma_{\hat{j}}|}{n^{2}|\sigma|^{2}}(\vec{n}_{i}\vec{n}_{j}^{\top})(\mathbf{f}_{i}\mathbf{f}_{j}^{\top}) (3.21)

(3.22)

|σi^|=1n−1∑[vi,vj]∈𝕊1​(σ)|σi^​j^|hiσcotθi​jσ.\displaystyle|\sigma_{\hat{i}}|=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{[v_{i},v_{j}]\in\mathbb{S}_{1}(\sigma)}|\sigma_{\hat{i}\hat{j}}|h_{i}^{\sigma}\cot\theta_{ij}^{\sigma}. (3.24)

Substituting (3.23) and (3.24) into (3.22), we have

‖∇f‖F2\displaystyle\|\nabla f\|_{F}^{2} =1|σ|​∑i=0n∑[vi,vj]∈𝕊1​(σ)1n⁡(n−1)|σi^​j^|cot⁡θi​jσ​𝐟i​j​𝐟j⊤=1|σ|​∑[vi,vj]∈𝕊1​(σ)w~i​jσ​𝐟i​j​𝐟i⊤.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\sigma|}\sum_{i=0}^{n}\sum_{[v_{i},v_{j}]\in\mathbb{S}_{1}(\sigma)}\frac{1}{n(n-1)}|\sigma_{\hat{i}\hat{j}}|\cot\theta_{ij}^{\sigma}\mathbf{f}_{ij}\mathbf{f}_{j}^{\top}=\frac{1}{|\sigma|}\sum_{[v_{i},v_{j}]\in\mathbb{S}_{1}(\sigma)}\tilde{w}_{ij}^{\sigma}\mathbf{f}_{ij}\mathbf{f}_{i}^{\top}. (3.25)

As a result,

ED​(f)=\displaystyle E_{D}(f)= 1n​∫ℳ‖∇f‖F2​𝑑s=1n​∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)‖∇f‖F2​|σ|\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\int_{\mathcal{M}}\|\nabla f\|_{F}^{2}ds=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\|\nabla f\|_{F}^{2}|\sigma| (3.26)
=\displaystyle= 1n​∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)∑i∈𝕊0​(σ)∑[vi,vj]∈𝕊1​(σ)w~i​jσ​𝐟i​j​𝐟i⊤=1n​∑i=1N∑[vi,vj]∈𝕊1​(ℳ)w~i​j​𝐟i​j​𝐟i⊤=1n​trace​(𝐟⊤​LD​𝐟).\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\sum_{i\in\mathbb{S}_{0}(\sigma)}\sum_{[v_{i},v_{j}]\in\mathbb{S}_{1}(\sigma)}\tilde{w}_{ij}^{\sigma}\mathbf{f}_{ij}\mathbf{f}_{i}^{\top}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{[v_{i},v_{j}]\in\mathbb{S}_{1}(\mathcal{M})}\tilde{w}_{ij}\mathbf{f}_{ij}\mathbf{f}_{i}^{\top}=\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{f}^{\top}L_{D}\mathbf{f}). (3.27)

∎

One can see that LDL_{D} has the identical sparse structure to LV​(f)L_{V}(f) in (3.9a). We further let LD​(f)L_{D}(f) be the Laplacian matrix defined on f⁡(ℳ)f(\mathcal{M}), as like LDL_{D} in (3.14). The cotangent weight of LD​(f)L_{D}(f) is w~i​j(f)=1n⁡(n−1)∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ):{vi,vj}⊂σ|f(σi^​j^)|cotθi​jσ(f).\tilde{w}_{ij}(f)=\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M}):\{v_{i},v_{j}\}\subset\sigma}|f(\sigma_{\hat{i}\hat{j}})|\cot\theta_{ij}^{\sigma}(f). Then, a representation of |f⁡(ℳ)||f(\mathcal{M})| and its gradient associated with LD​(f)L_{D}(f) is as in the following lemma.

Lemma 2.

The volume of the discrete nn-manifold f⁡(ℳ)f(\mathcal{M}) and its gradient with respect to 𝐟\mathbf{f} can be represented as

|f⁡(ℳ)|=1n​trace​(𝐟⊤​LD​(f)​𝐟),\displaystyle|f(\mathcal{M})|=\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{f}^{\top}L_{D}(f)\mathbf{f}), (3.28)
∇𝐟|f⁡(ℳ)|=LD​(f)​𝐟.\displaystyle\nabla_{\mathbf{f}}|f(\mathcal{M})|=L_{D}(f)\mathbf{f}. (3.29)
Proof.

By the definition of the nn-dimensional Dirichlet energy in (3.12), we have ED​(​i​d)|ℳ=|ℳ|E_{D}(\emph{id})\big|_{\mathcal{M}}=|\mathcal{M}|, where ​i​d\emph{id} is the identity map. Hence, for the discrete nn-manifold, by using the discrete formula (3.13), it follows that

|f⁡(ℳ)|=ED​(​i​d)|f⁡(ℳ):=1n​trace​(𝐟⊤​LD​(f)​𝐟).\displaystyle|f(\mathcal{M})|=E_{D}(\emph{id})\big|_{f(\mathcal{M})}:=\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{f}^{\top}L_{D}(f)\mathbf{f}). (3.30)

This proves the formula (3.28). On the other hand, from the formula (1) in [4], that is,

∇vi|σ|=1n⁡(n−1)∑[vi,vj]∈𝕊1​(σ)|σi^​j^|cotθi​jσvi​j=∑[vi,vj]∈𝕊1​(σ)w~i​jσvi​j,\displaystyle\nabla_{v_{i}}|\sigma|=\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{[v_{i},v_{j}]\in\mathbb{S}_{1}(\sigma)}|\sigma_{\hat{i}\hat{j}}|\cot\theta_{ij}^{\sigma}v_{ij}=\sum_{[v_{i},v_{j}]\in\mathbb{S}_{1}(\sigma)}\tilde{w}_{ij}^{\sigma}v_{ij}, (3.31)

we have

∇𝐟i|f(σ)|=∑[vi,vj]∈𝕊1​(σ)w~i​jσ(f)𝐟i​j,i=1,2,⋯,N.\displaystyle\nabla_{\mathbf{f}_{i}}|f(\sigma)|=\sum_{[{v}_{i},{v}_{j}]\in\mathbb{S}_{1}(\sigma)}\tilde{w}_{ij}^{\sigma}(f)\mathbf{f}_{ij},~i=1,2,\cdots,N. (3.32)

It follows that

∇𝐟i|f⁡(ℳ)|\displaystyle\nabla_{\mathbf{f}_{i}}|f(\mathcal{M})| =∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)∇𝐟i|f(σ)|=∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)∑[vi,vj]∈𝕊1​(σ)w~i​jσ(f)𝐟i​j,i=1,2,⋯,N.\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\nabla_{\mathbf{f}_{i}}|f(\sigma)|=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\sum_{[v_{i},v_{j}]\in\mathbb{S}_{1}(\sigma)}\tilde{w}_{ij}^{\sigma}(f)\mathbf{f}_{ij},~i=1,2,\cdots,N. (3.33)

Stacking these equations from 11 to NN, (3.29) is obtained. ∎

We can see that the definition of the volumetric stretch energy in (3.8) and the volume representation in (3.28) only differ in the cotangent weights in the Laplacian matrices LD​(f)L_{D}(f) and LV​(f)L_{V}(f). More specifically, the edge weights differ in a product of the stretch factor in (3.7). That is, wi​jσ​(f)=w~i​jσ​(f)σμ,f−1​(σ)w_{ij}^{\sigma}(f)=\frac{\tilde{w}_{ij}^{\sigma}(f)}{\sigma_{\mu,f^{-1}}(\sigma)}. Using this equality, we can provide a simple representation of the volumetric stretch energy functional in (3.8).

Theorem 3.

The volumetric stretch energy functional in (3.8) can be formulated as

EV​(f)=∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)|f⁡(σ)|2μ⁡(σ).\displaystyle E_{V}(f)=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\frac{|f(\sigma)|^{2}}{\mu(\sigma)}. (3.34)
Proof.

Split ℳ\mathcal{M} by its nn-simplex {σ}\{\sigma\} and consider the volumetric stretch energy on σ\sigma, then the volumetric stretch energy can also be splitted as

EV​(f)=∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)EV​(f)|σ.\displaystyle E_{V}(f)=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}E_{V}(f)\big|_{\sigma}. (3.35)

From (3.30) we have ED​(​i​d)|f⁡(σ)=|f⁡(σ)|E_{D}(\emph{id})\big|_{f(\sigma)}=|f(\sigma)|. Hence,

EV​(f)|σ\displaystyle E_{V}(f)\big|_{\sigma} =1n​∑[vi,vj]∈𝕊1​(σ)wi​jσ​(f)​‖𝐟i​j‖2=1n​σμ,f−1​(σ)​∑[vi,vj]∈𝕊1​(σ)w~i​jσ​(f)​‖𝐟i​j‖2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{[v_{i},v_{j}]\in\mathbb{S}_{1}(\sigma)}w_{ij}^{\sigma}(f)\|\mathbf{f}_{ij}\|^{2}=\frac{1}{n\sigma_{\mu,f^{-1}}(\sigma)}\sum_{[v_{i},v_{j}]\in\mathbb{S}_{1}(\sigma)}\tilde{w}_{ij}^{\sigma}(f)\|\mathbf{f}_{ij}\|^{2} (3.36)
=|f⁡(σ)|n​μ​(σ)​trace​(𝐟⊤​LD​(f)​𝐟)=|f⁡(σ)|μ⁡(σ)​ED​(i​d)|f⁡(σ)=|f⁡(σ)|2μ⁡(σ).\displaystyle=\frac{|f(\sigma)|}{n\mu(\sigma)}\mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{f}^{\top}L_{D}(f)\mathbf{f})=\frac{|f(\sigma)|}{\mu(\sigma)}E_{D}(id)\big|_{f(\sigma)}=\frac{|f(\sigma)|^{2}}{\mu(\sigma)}. (3.37)

Combining (3.35) with (3.37), (3.34) is obtained. ∎

Theorem 3 unifies the continuous and discrete nn-VSE and reveals that the discrete nn-VSE is formulated by the volumes of the original simplices σ\sigma and the image simplices f⁡(σ)f(\sigma). Next, we propose the discrete case of Theorem 1 for the lower bound of the nn-VSE, which is the foundation of our method. Different from Theorem 1, in the discrete case, the volume of the nn-ball is not a constant. Hence, we must add a constraint that f⁡(ℳ)f(\mathcal{M}) is a constant.

Theorem 4.

Let ℳ⊆ℝn\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be a discrete nn-manifold to be topologically equivalent to 𝔹n\mathbb{B}^{n} and μ⁡(⋅)\mu(\cdot) be the measure defined in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Let

Sf={EV(f)|f:ℳ→𝔹n is orientation preserving and piecewise affine with ∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)|f(σ)|=C,f(∂ℳ)=𝕊n−1}.\displaystyle S_{f}=\left\{E_{V}(f)~|~f:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{B}^{n}\text{ is orientation preserving and piecewise affine with }\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}|f(\sigma)|=C,f(\partial\mathcal{M})=\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\right\}. (3.38)

Then we have

  • (i)

    min⁡Sf≥C2∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)μ⁡(σ)\min S_{f}\geq\frac{C^{2}}{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\mu(\sigma)};

  • (ii)

    f∗=argminSf=C2∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)μ⁡(σ)f^{*}=\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}S_{f}=\frac{C^{2}}{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\mu(\sigma)} if and only if f∗f^{*} is volume-/mass-preserving, i.e., |f∗​(σ)|∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)|f∗​(σ)|=μ⁡(σ)∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)μ⁡(σ)\frac{|f^{*}(\sigma)|}{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}|f^{*}(\sigma)|}=\frac{\mu(\sigma)}{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\mu(\sigma)}, for each σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M}).

Proof.

Let m:=#​(𝕊n​(ℳ))m:=\#\big(\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})\big). Treating the volumes |f⁡(σ)||f(\sigma)| as variables, (3.34) is temporarily represented as

EV​(ξ)=∑i=1mξi2μ⁡(σi),ξ=(ξ1,ξ2,⋯,ξm)∈ℝ+m,\displaystyle E_{V}(\xi)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\xi_{i}^{2}}{\mu(\sigma_{i})},\hskip 9.24994pt\xi=(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\cdots,\xi_{m})\in\mathbb{R}^{m}_{+}, (3.39)

For the optimization problem

minξSξ≡{EV(ξ)|∑i=1mξi=C,ξi≥0,i=1,2,⋯,m},\displaystyle\min_{\xi}S_{\xi}\equiv\left\{E_{V}(\xi)~\left|~\sum_{i=1}^{m}\xi_{i}=C,~\xi_{i}\geq 0,~i=1,2,\cdots,m\right.\right\}, (3.40)

its Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) equation is

2​ξiμ⁡(σi)+λ=0,i=1,2,⋯,m.\displaystyle\frac{2\xi_{i}}{\mu(\sigma_{i})}+\lambda=0,\hskip 9.24994pti=1,2,\cdots,m. (3.41)

By the total volume constraints ∑i=1mξi=C\sum_{i=1}^{m}\xi_{i}=C, we have λ=−2​C∑i=1mμ⁡(σi)\lambda=-\frac{2C}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mu(\sigma_{i})} and ξi=C​μ​(σi)∑i=1mμ⁡(σi)\xi_{i}=\frac{C\mu(\sigma_{i})}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mu(\sigma_{i})}. That is

ξi∑i=1mξi=μ⁡(σi)∑i=1mμ⁡(σi),i=1,2,⋯,m.\displaystyle\frac{\xi_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\xi_{i}}=\frac{\mu(\sigma_{i})}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mu(\sigma_{i})},\hskip 9.24994pti=1,2,\cdots,m. (3.42)

Additionally, the problem (3.40) is convex, whose objective function and feasible region are all convex. Therefore, the solution of KKT equation (3.41) is the minimizer of the optimization problem (3.40) and hence min⁡Sξ=C2∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)μ⁡(σ)\min S_{\xi}=\frac{C^{2}}{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\mu(\sigma)}. Since 𝒮f⊆𝒮ξ\mathcal{S}_{f}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{\xi}, (i) min⁡Sf≥C2∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)μ⁡(σ)\min S_{f}\geq\frac{C^{2}}{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\mu(\sigma)} is obtained. Meanwhile, (3.42) demonstrates the volume-/mass-preserving property. As a consequence, f∗=argminSff^{*}=\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}S_{f} attains the lower bound C2∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)μ⁡(σ)\frac{C^{2}}{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\mu(\sigma)} if and only if |f∗​(σ)|∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)|f∗​(σ)|=μ⁡(σ)∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)μ⁡(σ),i=1,2,⋯,m\frac{|f^{*}(\sigma)|}{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}|f^{*}(\sigma)|}=\frac{\mu(\sigma)}{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\mu(\sigma)},i=1,2,\cdots,m, which leads to (ii). ∎

Like the theorem 1 in the continuous case, (i) gives the lower bound of the discrete nn-VSE under the constraints in (3.38) and (ii) indicates that the discrete nn-VSE reaches the lower bound if and only if the resulting map is mass-preserving. Identically, the existence and uniqueness of the ideal discrete mass-preserving map from ℳ\mathcal{M} to a unit nn-ball 𝔹n\mathbb{B}^{n} are not theoretically guaranteed. Therefore, the minimum of EV​(f)E_{V}(f) cannot always reach the lower bound C2∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)μ⁡(σ)\frac{C^{2}}{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\mu(\sigma)}. Hence, we define the mass-preserving error of the map ff as

ε=EV​(f)−C2∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)μ⁡(σ),\displaystyle\varepsilon=E_{V}(f)-\frac{C^{2}}{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\mu(\sigma)}, (3.43)

and the discrete ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving map.

Definition 4.

A map f:ℳ→𝔹nf:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{B}^{n} is a discrete ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving map if ε=EV​(f)−C2∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)μ⁡(σ)\varepsilon=E_{V}(f)-\frac{C^{2}}{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\mu(\sigma)}.

For the discrete ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving map, we can also give the measurement of ε\varepsilon.

Theorem 5.

Let f:ℳ→𝔹f:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{B} be an orientation preserving and piecewise affine map with ∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)|f⁡(σ)|=C\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}|f(\sigma)|=C, f⁡(∂ℳ)=𝕊n−1f(\partial\mathcal{M})=\mathbb{S}^{n-1} and ε=EV​(f)−C2∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)μ⁡(σ)\varepsilon=E_{V}(f)-\frac{C^{2}}{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\mu(\sigma)} and

δ=(δ1,δ2,⋯),δi=|f⁡(σi)|/∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)|f⁡(σi)|μ⁡(σi)/∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)μ⁡(σ)−1,\displaystyle\delta=(\delta_{1},\delta_{2},\cdots),\hskip 9.24994pt\delta_{i}=\frac{\nicefrac{{|f(\sigma_{i})|}}{{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}|f(\sigma_{i})|}}}{\nicefrac{{\mu(\sigma_{i})}}{{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\mu(\sigma)}}}-1, (3.44)

Then

μmin​C2(∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)μ⁡(σ))2​‖δ‖22≤ε≤μmax​C2(∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)μ⁡(σ))2​‖δ‖22.\displaystyle\mu_{\text{min}}\frac{C^{2}}{\left(\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\mu(\sigma)\right)^{2}}\|\delta\|_{2}^{2}\leq\varepsilon\leq\mu_{\text{max}}\frac{C^{2}}{\left(\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\mu(\sigma)\right)^{2}}\|\delta\|_{2}^{2}. (3.45)

where μmin\mu_{\text{min}} and μmax\mu_{\text{max}} are the minimum and maximum of μ⁡(σ)\mu(\sigma) among all σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M}), respectively.

Proof.

Suppose m:=#​(𝕊n​(ℳ))m:=\#(\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})). Let

ξ~i=|f⁡(σi)|∑i=1m|f⁡(σi)|,μ~i=μ⁡(σi)∑i=1mμ⁡(σi),\displaystyle\tilde{\xi}_{i}=\frac{|f(\sigma_{i})|}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}|f(\sigma_{i})|},\hskip 9.24994pt\tilde{\mu}_{i}=\frac{\mu(\sigma_{i})}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mu(\sigma_{i})}, (3.46)
μ~max:=maxi⁡μ~i=μmax∑i=1mμ⁡(σi),\displaystyle\tilde{\mu}_{\text{max}}:=\max_{i}\tilde{\mu}_{i}=\frac{\mu_{\text{max}}}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mu(\sigma_{i})}, (3.47)
μ~min:=maxi⁡μ~i=μmin∑i=1mμ⁡(σi).\displaystyle\tilde{\mu}_{\text{min}}:=\max_{i}\tilde{\mu}_{i}=\frac{\mu_{\text{min}}}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mu(\sigma_{i})}. (3.48)

Then δi=ξ~i/μ~i−1\delta_{i}={\tilde{\xi}_{i}}/{\tilde{\mu}_{i}}-1 and

∑i=1mξ~i=∑i=1mμ~i=1.\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}\tilde{\xi}_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\tilde{\mu}_{i}=1. (3.49)

We have

ε=\displaystyle\varepsilon= EV​(f)−C2∑i=1mμ⁡(σi)=C2∑i=1mμ⁡(σi)​[∑i=1mμ~i​(δi+1)2−1]\displaystyle E_{V}(f)-\frac{C^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mu(\sigma_{i})}=\frac{C^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mu(\sigma_{i})}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}\tilde{\mu}_{i}(\delta_{i}+1)^{2}-1\right] (3.50)
=\displaystyle= C2∑i=1mμ⁡(σi)​∑i=1mμ~i​[(δi+1)2−1]=C2∑i=1mμ⁡(σi)​∑i=1mμ~i​δi2.\displaystyle\frac{C^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mu(\sigma_{i})}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\tilde{\mu}_{i}[(\delta_{i}+1)^{2}-1]=\frac{C^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mu(\sigma_{i})}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\tilde{\mu}_{i}\delta_{i}^{2}. (3.51)

Since μ~i>0\tilde{\mu}_{i}>0, we have

∑i=1mμ~i​δi2≤μ~max​∑i=1mδi2=μ~max​‖δ‖22,\sum_{i=1}^{m}\tilde{\mu}_{i}\delta_{i}^{2}\leq\tilde{\mu}_{\text{max}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\delta_{i}^{2}=\tilde{\mu}_{\text{max}}\|\delta\|_{2}^{2}, (3.52a)
∑i=1mμ~i​δi2≥μ~min​∑i=1mδi2=μ~min​‖δ‖22.\sum_{i=1}^{m}\tilde{\mu}_{i}\delta_{i}^{2}\geq\tilde{\mu}_{\text{min}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\delta_{i}^{2}=\tilde{\mu}_{\text{min}}\|\delta\|_{2}^{2}. (3.52b)

Plugging (3.51), (3.47) and (3.48) into (3.52a) and (3.52b), the inequality (3.45) is obtained. ∎

As like the continuous case, Theorem 5 shows that we can use ε\varepsilon to measure the mass-preservation of the map. Meanwhile, minimizing SfS_{f} in (3.38) is a feasible method to find the ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving map.

4 Volumetric Stretch Energy Minimization

We aim to achieve the nn-dimensional volumetric stretch energy minimization (nn-VSEM), specifically, minimize SfS_{f} in (3.38) to find the ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving map from the nn-manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} to the unit nn-ball 𝔹n\mathbb{B}^{n}. We rewrite this problem as following.

min𝐟EV​(f):=1n​trace​(𝐟⊤​LV​(f)​𝐟)s.t.∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)|f⁡(σ)|=Cf⁡(∂ℳ)=𝒮n−1\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{l@{}c@{\quad}l}&\min_{\mathbf{f}}\hfil\hskip 9.24994pt&E_{V}(f):=\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{f}^{\top}L_{V}(f)\mathbf{f})\\ &\text{s.t.}\hfil\hskip 9.24994pt&\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}|f(\sigma)|=C\\ &\hfil\hskip 9.24994pt&f(\partial\mathcal{M})=\mathcal{S}^{n-1}\end{array}

This is a large scale and nonlinear optimization problem. We divide this problem (4) into boundary and interior parts instead. Let

𝙱={i|vi∈𝕊0​(∂ℳ)},𝙸={i|vi∈𝕊0​(ℳ)∖𝕊0​(∂ℳ)},\displaystyle\mathtt{B}=\{i~|~v_{i}\in\mathbb{S}_{0}(\partial\mathcal{M})\},\hskip 9.24994pt\mathtt{I}=\{i~|~v_{i}\in\mathbb{S}_{0}(\mathcal{M})\setminus\mathbb{S}_{0}(\partial\mathcal{M})\}, (4.4)

and partition 𝐟\mathbf{f} according to the boundary index 𝙱\mathtt{B} and interior index 𝙸\mathtt{I} as 𝐟=[𝐟𝙱⊤,𝐟𝙸⊤]⊤\mathbf{f}=[\mathbf{f}_{\mathtt{B}}^{\top},\mathbf{f}_{\mathtt{I}}^{\top}]^{\top}. The boundary and interior subproblems are as following.

  • 1)

    Boundary subproblem: given a measure μ′\mu^{\prime} defined in ∂ℳ\partial\mathcal{M}, find the ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving map g:∂ℳ→𝒮n−1g:\partial\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{S}^{n-1} by solving

    min𝐠EV​(g):=1n−1​trace​(𝐠⊤​LV​(g)​𝐠)s.t.∑σ∈𝕊n−1​(∂ℳ)|g⁡(σ)|=C′‖𝐠i‖22=1,vi∈𝕊0​(∂ℳ)\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{l@{}c@{\quad}l}&\min_{\mathbf{g}}\hfil\hskip 9.24994pt&E_{V}(g):=\frac{1}{n-1}\mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{g}^{\top}L_{V}(g)\mathbf{g})\\ &\text{s.t.}\hfil\hskip 9.24994pt&\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n-1}(\partial\mathcal{M})}|g(\sigma)|=C^{\prime}\\ &\hfil\hskip 9.24994pt&\|\mathbf{g}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=1,v_{i}\in\mathbb{S}_{0}(\partial\mathcal{M})\end{array}
  • 2)

    Interior subproblem: fix the boundary map 𝐟𝙱=𝐠\mathbf{f}_{\mathtt{B}}=\mathbf{g} and find the ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving map f:ℳ→𝔹nf:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{B}^{n} by solving

    min𝐟𝙸⁡EV​(f):=1n​trace​(𝐟⊤​LV​(f)​𝐟).\displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{f}_{\mathtt{I}}}\hskip 9.24994ptE_{V}(f):=\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{f}^{\top}L_{V}(f)\mathbf{f}). (4.8)

In the boundary subproblem (1)), the constraint f⁡(∂ℳ)=𝒮n−1f(\partial\mathcal{M})=\mathcal{S}^{n-1} is replaced by a weaken constraint ‖𝐠i‖2=1\|\mathbf{g}_{i}\|^{2}=1, vi∈∂ℳv_{i}\in\partial\mathcal{M}. This subproblem is a relatively low scale problem compared with (4) since the number of the boundary vertices is much less than that of whole vertices generally. The boundary subproblem (1)) can be treated as an independent problem for the spherical ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving parameterizations from a genus-00 nn-manifold to the unit nn-hypersphere. This problem is to obtain a boundary map for the computation of the interior map. In the interior subproblem (4.8), the boundary vertices are fixed. By the divergence theorem, the volume of the nn-ball is determined by the enclosed surface. Hence, the volume of f⁡(ℳ)f(\mathcal{M}) is also fixed, that is, the volume sum constraint ∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)|f⁡(σ)|=C\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}|f(\sigma)|=C in (4) is directed satisfied. Hence, we face to an unconstrained optimization problem in the subproblem (4.8). As a consequence, we divide the large scale and nonlinear problem (4) into a low scale constrained subproblem and an high scale unconstrained subproblem. By the Theorem 4, the resulting map of the subproblems is the ideal ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving map. The mass-preserving error ε\varepsilon depends on the boundary subproblem (1)).

Remark 3.

Generally, the orientation preserving condition is satisfied for the solution to the subproblems (1)) and (4.8) in numerical experiments. Even if there are overlap nn-simplices, the number of them is little. In this case, a convex combination postprocess can eliminate the overlap nn-simplices with a tiny mass-preserving loss. Therefore, we ignore the orientation preserving condition in the computation.

4.1 Initial map for spherical parameterization

We first introduce the nn-dimensional Dirac map inspired by [8]. Then the initial map for the boundary subproblem (1)) is obtained by a north-south alternating iteration. The Dirac map in [8] is to compute spherical conformal parameterization of the genus-00 closed surface by solving an inhomogeneous Laplace-Beltrami equation. We consider the generalized n−1n-1 dimensional equation

−Δ∂ℳ​g=(∂∂u1,∂∂u2,⋯,∂∂un−1)​δp\displaystyle-\Delta_{\partial\mathcal{M}}g=\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{1}},\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{2}},\cdots,\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{n-1}}\right)\delta_{p} (4.9)

where pp is a point on ∂ℳ\partial\mathcal{M}, δp\delta_{p} is Dirac delta function on pp, (u1,u2,⋯,un−1)(u_{1},u_{2},\cdots,u_{n-1}) is a local orthogonal coordinate on the neighborhood of pp and ∂∂ui\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{i}} is the directional differential with respect to uiu_{i}. The weak formulation of (4.9) for the test function hh is

∫∂ℳ⟨∇∂ℳg,∇∂ℳh⟩​𝑑s=⟨(∂∂u1,∂∂u2,⋯,∂∂un−1),h⟩|p,\displaystyle\int_{\partial\mathcal{M}}\big\langle\nabla_{\partial\mathcal{M}}g,\nabla_{\partial\mathcal{M}}h\big\rangle ds=\Big\langle\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{1}},\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{2}},\cdots,\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{n-1}}\right),h\Big\rangle\Big|_{p}, (4.10)

Here ∂ℳ\partial\mathcal{M} is a simplical (n−1)(n-1)-complex. gg and hh are piecewise affine map induced by 𝐠\mathbf{g} and 𝐡\mathbf{h}, respectively. (i) For the left hand term, similar to the proof of Lemma 1, it can be easily verified that

∫∂ℳ⟨∇∂ℳg,∇∂ℳh⟩​𝑑s=trace⁡(𝐡⊤​LD​𝐠),\displaystyle\int_{\partial\mathcal{M}}\big\langle\nabla_{\partial\mathcal{M}}g,\nabla_{\partial\mathcal{M}}h\big\rangle ds=\mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{h}^{\top}L_{D}\mathbf{g}), (4.11)

where LDL_{D} is defined in (3.14).

(ii) For the right hand term, suppose that pp is in τp=[v0,v1,⋯,vn−1]\tau_{p}=[v_{0},v_{1},\cdots,v_{n-1}]. Then we need to find an orthogonal coordinate in τp\tau_{p}, which can be constructed by the QR decomposition of matrix

[v10⊤,v20⊤,⋯,v(n−1)​0⊤]=Q​R,\displaystyle[v_{10}^{\top},v_{20}^{\top},\cdots,v_{(n-1)0}^{\top}]=QR, (4.12)

where Q=[q1,q2,⋯,qn−1]∈ℝn×(n−1)Q=[q_{1},q_{2},\cdots,q_{n-1}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-1)} is the required orthogonal coordinates. Hence, the right term becomes

⟨(∂∂u1,∂∂u2,⋯,∂∂un−1),h⟩|p=∑i=1n−1∂h(i)∂qi|p=trace⁡(∇h|p​Q).\displaystyle\Big\langle\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{1}},\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{2}},\cdots,\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{n-1}}\right),h\Big\rangle\Big|_{p}=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\left.\frac{\partial h^{(i)}}{\partial q_{i}}\right|_{p}=\mathrm{trace}(\nabla h|_{p}Q). (4.13)

Combining (4.11) and (4.13), the weak formulation (4.10) becomes

trace⁡(𝐡⊤​LD​𝐠)=trace⁡(∇h|p​Q),\displaystyle\mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{h}^{\top}L_{D}\mathbf{g})=\mathrm{trace}(\nabla h|_{p}Q), (4.14)

for the test function hh. Letting

h⁡(v)={ej⊤,v=vi,0,v≠vi,v∈𝕊0(∂ℳ),\displaystyle h(v)=\begin{cases}e_{j}^{\top},&v=v_{i},\\ 0,&v\neq v_{i},v\in\mathbb{S}_{0}(\partial\mathcal{M}),\end{cases} (4.15)

for i=1,⋯,Ni=1,\cdots,N and j=1,2,⋯,nj=1,2,\cdots,n, we have

LD​𝐠=𝐛,\displaystyle L_{D}\mathbf{g}=\mathbf{b}, (4.16)

where

[𝐛]i={0,vi∉𝕊0​(τp),∇αiQ,vi∈𝕊0​(τp).\displaystyle[\mathbf{b}]_{i}=\begin{cases}0,&v_{i}\notin\mathbb{S}_{0}(\tau_{p}),\\ \nabla\alpha_{i}Q,&v_{i}\in\mathbb{S}_{0}(\tau_{p}).\end{cases} (4.17)

By the barycentre coodinates formula in (3.19), letting R=[r1,r2,⋯,rn−1]R=[r_{1},r_{2},\cdots,r_{n-1}] in (4.12) and r0=0r_{0}=0, we have

∇αiQ=1|τp|∑j≠iw~i​jτpvi​jQ=1|τp|∑j≠iw~i​jτp(ri−rj)⊤.\displaystyle\nabla\alpha_{i}Q=\frac{1}{|\tau_{p}|}\sum_{j\neq i}\tilde{w}_{ij}^{\tau_{p}}v_{ij}Q=\frac{1}{|\tau_{p}|}\sum_{j\neq i}\tilde{w}_{ij}^{\tau_{p}}(r_{i}-r_{j})^{\top}. (4.18)

To solve the linear system (4.16) under the spherical constraint, we introduce the (n−1)(n-1)-dimensional stereographic projection Π:𝒮n−1→ℝ¯n−1\Pi:\mathcal{S}^{n-1}\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}^{n-1}, defined as

Π⁡(𝐟i)=[𝐟i11−𝐟in,𝐟i21−𝐟in,⋯,𝐟in−11−𝐟in],\displaystyle\Pi(\mathbf{f}_{i})=\left[\frac{\mathbf{f}_{i}^{1}}{1-\mathbf{f}_{i}^{n}},\frac{\mathbf{f}_{i}^{2}}{1-\mathbf{f}_{i}^{n}},\cdots,\frac{\mathbf{f}_{i}^{n-1}}{1-\mathbf{f}_{i}^{n}}\right], (4.19)

for 𝐟i=[𝐟i1,𝐟i2,⋯,𝐟in]\mathbf{f}_{i}=[\mathbf{f}_{i}^{1},\mathbf{f}_{i}^{2},\cdots,\mathbf{f}_{i}^{n}]. Let h=Π∘gh=\Pi\circ g and 𝐡=Π⁡(𝐠)\mathbf{h}=\Pi(\mathbf{g}). Consider the linear system

LD​𝐡=𝐛.\displaystyle L_{D}\mathbf{h}=\mathbf{b}. (4.20)

The Laplacian matrix LDL_{D} is singular, which has a eigenpair (0,𝟏)(0,\mathbf{1}), which means that it is unique up to translation. Hence, we can fix a point 𝐡i\mathbf{h}_{i} to solve it. Since the stereographic projection is a conformal map, the map g:=Π−1∘hg:=\Pi^{-1}\circ h is the solution of (4.16). Algorithm 1 shows the computation of the (n−1)(n-1)-dimensional spherical Dirac map.

Inspired from SEM algorithm in [20], we can apply the stereographic projection to design a north-south alternating iteration algorithm in 2. The resulting map of this algorithm has small ε\varepsilon. Hence, it can provide an ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving map as the initial map and the sum of the volume C′C^{\prime} for our proposed algorithm.

4.2 Spherical ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving parameterization

The spherical ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving parameterization is achieved by solving the spherical subproblem (1)) as following,

min𝐠EV​(g):=1n−1​trace​(𝐠⊤​LV​(g)​𝐠)s.t.∑σ∈𝕊n−1​(∂ℳ)|g⁡(σ)|=C′‖𝐠i‖22=1,vi∈𝕊0​(∂ℳ)\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{l@{}c@{\quad}l}&\min_{\mathbf{g}}\hfil\hskip 9.24994pt&E_{V}(g):=\frac{1}{n-1}\mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{g}^{\top}L_{V}(g)\mathbf{g})\\ &\text{s.t.}\hfil\hskip 9.24994pt&\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n-1}(\partial\mathcal{M})}|g(\sigma)|=C^{\prime}\\ &\hfil\hskip 9.24994pt&\|\mathbf{g}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=1,v_{i}\in\mathbb{S}_{0}(\partial\mathcal{M})\end{array}

We adopt the Newton method to this problem. We first present a theorem for the gradient of the nn-VSE.

Theorem 6.

The gradient of volumetric stretch energy functional in (3.8) can be formulated as

∇EV​(f)=2​LV​(f)​𝐟.\displaystyle\nabla E_{V}(f)=2L_{V}(f)\mathbf{f}. (4.25)
Proof.

By Theorem 3, we have

EV​(f)=∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)|f⁡(σ)|2μ⁡(σ).\displaystyle E_{V}(f)=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\frac{|f(\sigma)|^{2}}{\mu(\sigma)}. (4.26)

Using the chain rule, we can represent its gradient as

∇EV(f)=2∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)|f⁡(σ)|μ⁡(σ)∇|f(σ)|.\displaystyle\nabla E_{V}(f)=2\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\frac{|f(\sigma)|}{\mu(\sigma)}\nabla|f(\sigma)|. (4.27)

Plugging the gradient formula of |f⁡(σ)||f(\sigma)| in (3.32) into it, we have

∂∂𝐟i​EV​(f)=\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\mathbf{f}_{i}}E_{V}(f)= 2∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)∑[vi,vj]∈𝕊1​(σ)[1n⁡(n−1)|f⁡(σ−i​j)|σμ,f−1​(σ)cotθi​jσ(f)]𝐟i​j\displaystyle 2\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\sum_{[v_{i},v_{j}]\in\mathbb{S}_{1}(\sigma)}\left[\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\frac{|f(\sigma_{-ij})|}{\sigma_{\mu,f^{-1}}(\sigma)}\cot\theta_{ij}^{\sigma}(f)\right]\mathbf{f}_{ij} (4.28)
=\displaystyle= 2​∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)∑[vi,vj]∈𝕊1​(σ)wi​jσ​(f)​(𝐟i−𝐟j)=2​∑[vi,vj]∈𝕊1​(ℳ)wi​j​(f)​(𝐟i−𝐟j)\displaystyle 2\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\sum_{[v_{i},v_{j}]\in\mathbb{S}_{1}(\sigma)}w_{ij}^{\sigma}(f)(\mathbf{f}_{i}-\mathbf{f}_{j})=2\sum_{[v_{i},v_{j}]\in\mathbb{S}_{1}(\mathcal{M})}w_{ij}(f)(\mathbf{f}_{i}-\mathbf{f}_{j}) (4.29)
=\displaystyle= 2​ei⊤​LV​(f)​𝐟,\displaystyle 2e_{i}^{\top}L_{V}(f)\mathbf{f}, (4.30)

completing the proof. ∎

The gradient formula in (4.25) also holds for 𝒮n−1\mathcal{S}^{n-1} without loss of generality. Then, we consider the Lagrange multiplier,

L⁡(𝐠,λ,𝒔)=EV​(g)+λ⁡(∑σ∈𝕊n−1​(∂ℳ)|g⁡(σ)|−C′)+12​∑i𝒔i​(‖𝐠i‖22−1).\displaystyle L(\mathbf{g},\lambda,\bm{s})=E_{V}(g)+\lambda(\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n-1}(\partial\mathcal{M})}|g(\sigma)|-C^{\prime})+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\bm{s}_{i}(\|\mathbf{g}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}-1). (4.31)

From Lemma 2 and Theorem 6, the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker equations are

2​LV​(g)​𝐠+λ​LD​(g)​𝐠+diag⁡(𝒔)​𝐠=0,\displaystyle 2L_{V}(g)\mathbf{g}+\lambda L_{D}(g)\mathbf{g}+\mathrm{diag}(\bm{s})\mathbf{g}=0, (4.32)
∑σ∈𝕊n−1​(∂ℳ)|g⁡(σ)|−C′=0,\displaystyle\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n-1}(\partial\mathcal{M})}|g(\sigma)|-C^{\prime}=0, (4.33)
12​(‖𝐠‖2−1)=0,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}(\|\mathbf{g}\|^{2}-1)=0, (4.34)

where ‖𝐠‖\|\mathbf{g}\| means the column vector with the ii-th entry being ‖𝐠i‖2\|\mathbf{g}_{i}\|_{2}. For this primal-dual problem, the Newton step is obtained by solving the linear system

[∇vec​(𝐠)2​Lvec​(LD​(g)​𝐠)cdiag​(𝐠)vec​(LD​(g)​𝐠)⊤00cdiag​(𝐠)⊤00]​[Δ​vec​(𝐠)Δ​λΔ​𝒔]=−[vec​(2​LV​(g)​𝐠+λ​LD​(g)​𝐠+𝐠​diag​(𝒔))∑σ∈𝕊n−1​(∂ℳ)|g⁡(σ)|−C′‖𝐠‖2−1],\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}\nabla_{\text{vec}(\mathbf{g})}^{2}L&\text{vec}(L_{D}(g)\mathbf{g})&\text{cdiag}(\mathbf{g})\\ \text{vec}(L_{D}(g)\mathbf{g})^{\top}&0&0\\ \text{cdiag}(\mathbf{g})^{\top}&0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta\text{vec}(\mathbf{g})\\ \Delta\lambda\\ \Delta\bm{s}\end{bmatrix}=-\begin{bmatrix}\text{vec}(2L_{V}(g)\mathbf{g}+\lambda L_{D}(g)\mathbf{g}+\mathbf{g}\mathrm{diag}(\bm{s}))\\ \sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n-1}(\partial\mathcal{M})}|g(\sigma)|-C^{\prime}\\ \|\mathbf{g}\|^{2}-1\end{bmatrix}, (4.35)

in which vec means the vectorization of a matrix, cdiag​(𝐠)\text{cdiag}(\mathbf{g}) is a block diagonal matrix with its ii-th block being 𝐠i\mathbf{g}^{i}, and ∇vec​(𝐠)2​L\nabla_{\text{vec}(\mathbf{g})}^{2}L is the Hessian matrix with respect to vec​(𝐠){\text{vec}(\mathbf{g})} of the Lagrange multiplier (4.31). It can be verified that the Hessian matrix ∇𝐠2​L\nabla_{\mathbf{g}}^{2}L is of identical sparsity as 𝟏(n−1)×(n−1)⊗LD\mathbf{1}_{(n-1)\times(n-1)}\otimes L_{D}. Here we can estimate it by finite difference method. Hence, we propose the Algorithm 3 for the (n−1)(n-1)-spherical mass-preserving parameterization.

4.3 Ball ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving parameterization

The ball ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving parameterization need a fixed boundary map according to the above discussion. However, a sliver nn-manifold may lead to a boundary map with low quality in the numerical perspective. To obtain a better boundary map, we stretch the boundary vertices V𝙱:=[v1⊤,v2⊤,⋯,vm⊤]⊤V_{\mathtt{B}}:=[v_{1}^{\top},v_{2}^{\top},\cdots,v_{m}^{\top}]^{\top} along the principal axes, such that the nn-manifold becomes a ball-like shape. Generally, this stretched nn-manifold may result in a better boundary map. Moreover, this stretch transformation is also a mass-preserving map. Specifically, the stretch transformation is obtained by solving the eigenvalue problem

V~𝙱⊤​V~𝙱​X=X​Λ,\displaystyle\tilde{V}_{\mathtt{B}}^{\top}\tilde{V}_{\mathtt{B}}X=X\Lambda, (4.37)

where V~𝙱=(I−1m​𝟏𝟏⊤)​V𝙱\tilde{V}_{\mathtt{B}}=(I-\frac{1}{m}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top})V_{\mathtt{B}} with m=#​𝙱m=\#\mathtt{B}, X=[x1,⋯,xn]X=[x_{1},\cdots,x_{n}] is the directions of the principal axes and Λ=[λ1,⋯,λn]\Lambda=[\lambda_{1},\cdots,\lambda_{n}] are the square of length of the principal axes. Then V~𝙱​X​Λ−12\tilde{V}_{\mathtt{B}}X\Lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}} are the vertices of the ball-like manifold. The solution of this problem can be calculated by the singular value decomposition of V~𝙱\tilde{V}_{\mathtt{B}}. We can verify that the left singular vector U=V~𝙱​X​Λ−12U=\tilde{V}_{\mathtt{B}}X\Lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}}.

After the computation of the boundary map f𝙱=𝐠f_{\mathtt{B}}=\mathbf{g}, we focus on the ball subproblem (4.8) as following,

min𝐟𝙸⁡EV​(f):=1n​trace​(𝐟⊤​LV​(f)​𝐟).\displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{f}_{\mathtt{I}}}\hskip 9.24994ptE_{V}(f):=\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{f}^{\top}L_{V}(f)\mathbf{f}). (4.38)

Different from the spherical subproblem, since the boundary vertices are fixed, the volume of the enclosed region of the boundary surface is determined. Hence, the conditions in (3.38) are satisfied. By the Theorem 4, the solution to the unconstrained problem (4.38) is the target ε\varepsilon-mass-preserving map.

Partition LV​(f)L_{V}(f) according to the boundary index 𝙱\mathtt{B} and interior index 𝙸\mathtt{I}

LV​(f)=[[LV​(f)]𝙱𝙱[LV​(f)]𝙱𝙸[LV​(f)]𝙸𝙱[LV​(f)]𝙸𝙸].\displaystyle L_{V}(f)=\begin{bmatrix}[L_{V}(f)]_{\mathtt{B}\mathtt{B}}&[L_{V}(f)]_{\mathtt{B}\mathtt{I}}\\ [L_{V}(f)]_{\mathtt{I}\mathtt{B}}&[L_{V}(f)]_{\mathtt{I}\mathtt{I}}\end{bmatrix}. (4.39)

From the Theorem 6, the subproblem (4.38) reaches the minimum if [LV​(f)​𝐟]𝙸=0[L_{V}(f)\mathbf{f}]_{\mathtt{I}}=0, that is,

[LV​(f)]𝙸𝙸​𝐟𝙸=−[LV​(f)]𝙸𝙱​𝐟𝙱.\displaystyle[L_{V}(f)]_{\mathtt{I}\mathtt{I}}\mathbf{f}_{\mathtt{I}}=-[L_{V}(f)]_{\mathtt{I}\mathtt{B}}\mathbf{f}_{\mathtt{B}}. (4.40)

This motivate us to solve the linear system (4.40) to compute the interior vertices 𝐟𝙸(i)\mathbf{f}_{\mathtt{I}}^{(i)} by the Laplacian matrix LV​(f(i−1))L_{V}(f^{(i-1)}) at the ii-th iterative step. We summarize this strategy in Algorithm 4.

5 Numerical Experiments

In this section, we indicate the numerical performance of our proposed algorithms for the nn-manifold ℳ\mathcal{M} and the (n−1)(n-1)-manifold. We mainly focus on the 33-dimensional and 44-dimensional cases. The 33-dimensional surface benchmarks are taken from AIM@SHAPE shape repository (http://visionair.ge.imati.cnr.it/ontologies/shapes/), the Stanford 3D scanning repository (http://graphics.stanford.edu/data/3Dscanrep), and TurboSquid (https://www.turbosquid.com/). The 33-dimensional solid benchmarks are generated with the above surfaces by the builtin function generateMesh of MATLAB. The 44-dimensional benchmarks are manually generated. All experimental programs are executed in MATLAB R2021a on a personal computer with a 2.50 GHz CPU and 64 GB RAM. We consider the volume-preserving map if no special illustration. In other words, the measures of the benchmarks are μ(⋅)=|⋅|\mu(\cdot)=|\cdot|.

5.1 Ellipsoid case

First, we give 33- and 44-ellipsoids as a special case for the nn-VSEM. Let En​(𝐚)E^{n}(\mathbf{a}) be a nn-ellipsoid with 𝐚i\mathbf{a}_{i} being the length of the ii-th axis. We can find that the map f∗:(v1,v2,⋯,vn)→(v1𝐚1,v2𝐚2,⋯,vn𝐚n)f^{*}:(v^{1},v^{2},\cdots,v^{n})\to\left(\frac{v_{1}}{\mathbf{a}_{1}},\frac{v_{2}}{\mathbf{a}_{2}},\cdots,\frac{v_{n}}{\mathbf{a}_{n}}\right) is a volume-preserving map. We aim to compute the this volume-preserving map f∗f^{*} to confirm the mass-preservation of nn-VSEM. It is worth noting that the boundary map f∗​(∂En​(𝐚))=𝒮n−1f^{*}(\partial E^{n}(\mathbf{a}))=\mathcal{S}^{n-1} is not a volume-preserving map. The ratio of the volume |f⁡(τ)|/|τ||f(\tau)|/|\tau| with τ=[v0,v1,⋯,vn−1]\tau=[v_{0},v_{1},\cdots,v_{n-1}] satisfies

|f∗​(τ)||τ|=|𝐟10∗∧𝐟20∗∧⋯∧𝐟n​0∗||v10∧v20∧⋯∧vn​0|=∑i=1n−1det([𝐟(i+1)​0∗⁣⊤,⋯,𝐟(n−1)​0∗⁣⊤,𝐟10∗⁣⊤,⋯,𝐟(i−1)​0∗⁣⊤])∑i=1n−1det([v(i+1)​0⊤,⋯,v(n−1)​0⊤,v10⊤,⋯,v(i−1)​0⊤]).\displaystyle\frac{|f^{*}(\tau)|}{|\tau|}=\frac{|\mathbf{f}_{10}^{*}\wedge\mathbf{f}_{20}^{*}\wedge\cdots\wedge\mathbf{f}_{n0}^{*}|}{|v_{10}\wedge v_{20}\wedge\cdots\wedge v_{n0}|}=\frac{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\det([\mathbf{f}_{(i+1)0}^{*\top},\cdots,\mathbf{f}_{(n-1)0}^{*\top},\mathbf{f}_{10}^{*\top},\cdots,\mathbf{f}_{(i-1)0}^{*\top}])}}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\det([v_{(i+1)0}^{\top},\cdots,v_{(n-1)0}^{\top},v_{10}^{\top},\cdots,v_{(i-1)0}^{\top}])}}. (5.1)

Hence, we choose μ′​(τ)=|τ||f∗​(τ)|\mu^{\prime}(\tau)=\frac{|\tau|}{|f^{*}(\tau)|} and C′=∑τ∈𝕊n−1​(∂ℳ)|f∗​(τ)|C^{\prime}=\sum_{\tau\in\mathbb{S}_{n-1}(\partial\mathcal{M})}|f^{*}(\tau)| for the boundary map in the Algorithm 3. The initial map is the exact solution with a perturbation 10−410^{-4}. Then we compute the map ff by the Algorithm 4 with the computed boundary map. Since the normalization for the ball-like shape in Algorithm 4 directly leads to the exact solution, we do not execute this normalization process to show the effect of the proposed algorithms. The Algorithm 3 converges within 2020 iterative steps and Algorithm 4 converges within 33 iterative steps. Table 1 shows the 33 and 44 dimensional ellipsoids for the experiment and the mass-preserving performances of Algorithm 3 and Algorithm 4, where #​𝙱\#\mathtt{B} and #​𝙸\#\mathtt{I} are the the number of the boundary and vertices vertices, respectively. And the definitions of ε\varepsilon and δ\delta are in (3.43) and (3.44), respectively. We can see that the measurements ε\varepsilon and δ\delta are closed to 10−1610^{-16}, which indicates that our proposed algorithms compute the mass-preserving parameterization numerically.

5.2 General cases

Now we focus on the general cases, which have not exact volume-preserving solutions. Hence, we compute the ε\varepsilon-volume-preserving parameterization with as small ε\varepsilon as possible. Figure 3 shows the 33 dimensional benchmarks and the projected surfaces along a direction of the 44 dimensional benchmarks. Table 2 demonstrates the basic information and the results of the proposed algorithms on the 33 and 44 dimensional benchmarks, where nn is the dimension of the manifolds. We set |∂ℳ|=|𝒮n−1||\partial\mathcal{M}|=|\mathcal{S}^{n-1}| and |ℳ|=|𝔹n||\mathcal{M}|=|\mathbb{B}^{n}| in the measurement ε\varepsilon for the better presentation and comparison.

From the Table 2, we can see that the proposed spherical and ball algorithms have well performances on the volume-preservation among all the benchmarks. For the boundary problem, the measurements ε\varepsilon are on the order 10−610^{-6} to 10−410^{-4} and the local relative error delta are from 10−710^{-7} to 10−510^{-5}. For the interior problem, the measurements ε\varepsilon are on the order 10−410^{-4} to 10−210^{-2} and the local relative error delta are 10−510^{-5} to 10−310^{-3}. For the 4 dimensional benchmarks, the measurements are slightly larger. Improving the accuracy of higher dimensional parameterizations is still worthy and significant work in the future. Additionally, the histograms in Figure 2 specifically show the distributions of the local volume ratios δi+1=|f⁡(σi)|/∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)|f⁡(σi)|μ⁡(σi)/∑σ∈𝕊n​(ℳ)μ⁡(σ)\delta_{i}+1=\frac{\nicefrac{{|f(\sigma_{i})|}}{{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}|f(\sigma_{i})|}}}{\nicefrac{{\mu(\sigma_{i})}}{{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathbb{S}_{n}(\mathcal{M})}\mu(\sigma)}}}. We can see that the ratios concentrate in 1 tightly, indicating the high volume-preservation of our proposed algorithms.

7 Conclusion

In this paper, we propose the nn-VSE functional to achieve the mass-preserving parameterization for the nn-manifold topologically equivalent to the nn-ball. The nn-VSE can be treated as the sum of the mass ratios among the manifold. We give a lower bound of the nn-VSE and proof that the nn-VSE reaches the lower bound if and only if the map is mass-preserving. This is the foundation of our proposed algorithms that aim to minimize the nn-VSE. In the discrete case, the nn-VSE is equivalent to the energies defined in [23, 20, 9] when n=2n=2 and n=3n=3. The discrete nn-VSE can be formulated as the quadratic form with respect to the Laplacian matrix and the gradient of the discrete nn-VSE is of the simple formulation, that is, the product of the Laplacian matrix and the image vertices. This property makes the nn-VSEM more practical. To compute the mass-preserving parameterization of the nn-manifold, we solve the boundary and interior subproblems by developing the spherical and the interior algorithms, respectively. The numerical experiment shows the high accuracy of our developed algorithms, especially for the 33-manifolds.

However, the efficiency and accuracy, especially for the higher dimensional manifolds, are not fully satisfactory. The high dimensional manifolds need more vertices and simplices to represent with high resolution, which makes the scale of the problem more huge. It is still a challenging problem.
